title: Jump Game
description: Brute force to optimized: recursively exploring every jump path versus tracking a single running maximum reach in one pass.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an array nums where nums[i] represents the maximum jump length from index i, starting at index 0, determine if you can reach the last index.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","nums, where nums[i] is the max jump length from index i"],["Output","true if the last index is reachable from index 0, false otherwise"],["Goal","Determine reachability in a single pass, tracking the farthest reachable index"],["Constraints","1 <= nums.length <= 10^4"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Maximum jump length from each position, reach the end?\"","Track the farthest reachable index in a single greedy pass"],["Only REACHABILITY matters, not the specific path taken","No need to track individual jump sequences, just the frontier of reachability"]]}

blocks.text: Since only whether the last index is reachable matters (not the specific sequence of jumps), tracking the single farthest index reachable so far, updated as each position is visited, is sufficient: if the current position is ever beyond this farthest reach, it means no earlier jump could get here, so the end is unreachable.

blocks.title: Analogy: Stepping Stones Across a River With Varying Jump Distances
blocks.text: Picture stepping stones across a river, where each stone lets you jump at most a certain distance further. Rather than tracking every possible path, you can just track the FARTHEST point reachable so far as you walk across; if you ever reach a stone beyond that farthest point without having stepped on it, you are stuck.

blocks.caption: Track the farthest reachable index; if the current index ever exceeds it, reaching the end is impossible

blocks.text: Result: true. From index 0 (jump up to 2), reach index 1 (jump up to 3), reaching index 4, the last index.

Before trying every possible sequence of jumps, notice that only the FARTHEST reachable index matters at any point, since reaching further is always at least as good as reaching less far, regardless of which specific path got you there.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: If the current index i is beyond the farthest reachable index tracked so far, no sequence of jumps from index 0 could have reached i, so the whole array is unreachable beyond this point.

Observation 2: Otherwise, index i IS reachable, and jumping from it can extend the farthest reachable index to i + nums[i] (if this is larger than the current farthest reach).

Observation 3: Processing indices left to right, updating this single farthest-reach value, correctly captures whether every subsequent index (up to and including the last) is reachable.

Observation 4: The moment the farthest reach reaches or exceeds the last index, success is guaranteed (though the loop can also simply continue and finish naturally, since past that point the check always passes).
This leads to a single pass: track the farthest reachable index; if the current index ever exceeds it, return false; otherwise, extend the farthest reach using the current index's jump length.
Recursively try every possible jump length from each index, checking if ANY resulting path reaches the last index.

items: From the current index, try every possible jump length from 1 up to nums[index].
Recursively check if any of the resulting positions can eventually reach the last index.
Return true if any recursive path succeeds, false if all fail.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Trying every possible jump length recursively explores every possible path directly.
This can revisit the same positions many times via different jump sequences, costing exponential time in the worst case.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: exponential in the worst case (each position can branch into up to nums[i] recursive calls).
Space: O(n) recursion depth.
Limitation: since only reachability (not the specific path) matters, tracking a single "farthest reachable index" value in one greedy pass achieves O(n) instead of exponential time.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why trying every jump path is unnecessary: the SPECIFIC sequence of jumps taken to reach some index never matters, only WHETHER it is reachable, and by how far a jump from it could extend reach.

The single greedy pass: maintain one value, the farthest index reachable so far; process indices left to right, and at each reachable index, extend this farthest reach using that index's jump length.

Detecting failure: if the current index ever exceeds the farthest reach tracked so far, it means no path could have reached this index, so the end is definitively unreachable.

The core idea: reduce the entire reachability question to tracking one running maximum, updated in a single linear pass.
Track a single "reach" value, initialized to 0. For each index i (left to right), if i exceeds reach, return false; otherwise, update reach to the maximum of its current value and i + nums[i].

blocks.caption: A single running "reach" value tracks the farthest index reachable so far

codes.python:
def can_jump(nums):
    reach = 0
    for i in range(len(nums)):
        if i > reach:                                # this index is unreachable
            return False
        reach = max(reach, i + nums[i])                # extend the farthest reach
    return True

blocks.text: The running "reach" value at any point in the pass correctly represents the farthest index reachable using ANY sequence of jumps from index 0 up through the indices already processed. If the current index ever exceeds this value, it proves no reachable earlier index could jump far enough to reach it, making the end definitively unreachable; otherwise, extending reach using the current (definitely reachable) index's jump length correctly maintains this invariant for the next index.

blocks.text: Jump Game is the foundational "track a single running frontier of reachability" greedy problem, a technique reused across the entire Jump Game family and many reachability problems.

items: Checking i >= reach instead of i > reach, which would incorrectly reject the exact boundary case where a jump lands exactly at the current farthest reach.
Trying to track the actual jump PATH instead of just the reach value, adding unnecessary complexity.

blocks.text: Explicitly stating "only reachability matters, not the specific path, so track just the farthest reach" clarifies why the greedy single-pass approach is both correct and sufficient.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "can you reach the end, given variable jump lengths from each position", think: track the single farthest reachable index in one greedy pass.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Recursive path exploration costs exponential time; the single-pass max-reach tracking approach costs O(n) time and O(1) space, the standard efficient solution.

items: Pattern: track a single running "farthest reachable index" in one greedy pass.
Core Idea: if the current index ever exceeds the farthest reach so far, the end is unreachable; otherwise, extend the reach using the current index's jump length.
Time: exponential for recursive path exploration, O(n) for the optimized single pass.
Space: O(n) recursion depth versus O(1) extra.
Most Important Observation: only reachability matters, not the specific jump sequence, so a single running maximum suffices.
Interview Difficulty: a foundational greedy reachability problem, the basis for the entire Jump Game family.
One line memory trick: track the farthest reach; fail if the current index ever exceeds it.
